standard.title: Design and make solutions
standard.description: generate, communicate and evaluate design ideas, and use materials, equipment and steps to safely make a solution for a purpose
standard.prior_knowledge: This is the first Design and Technologies process descriptor. Students have no prior design process experience assumed. They bring general play and construction experience. They have not yet framed design as purposeful — generating ideas for a specific purpose, communicating those ideas in a design form, making a solution, or evaluating against a purpose.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students generate and communicate at least one design idea for a purpose, use materials and equipment safely to make a solution, and evaluate what they made using personal preferences.

nodes.label: Identifying a purpose and generating ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a purpose for designing and making, and generate at least one idea for a solution
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a purpose for a design task (what problem or need is being addressed); generate at least one idea for a solution
nodes.typical_width: Identify a purpose for designing and making; generate and explore multiple ideas through drawing, modelling or describing; choose the most suitable idea with a reason
wider: Identify a real purpose from the school environment (e.g. sand blowing out of sandpit, birds getting into waste bins, accessibility needs at school) — generate ideas that directly address the identified purpose
Draw or model designs for bee hotels to attract native bees to the school garden — generate multiple ideas and choose one, changing perspectives from front view to plan view

response_modes.reason: Foundation students readily generate ideas but often skip connecting them to a purpose — the idea exists without a 'what is it for'. Multiple design contexts where the purpose is clearly defined before generating ideas builds the habit of purpose-grounded design thinking rather than open-ended construction play.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Real school-environment purposes (bee hotels, accessibility) make the purpose-idea connection genuinely substantive — students are solving a real problem rather than a notional one, which makes the design thinking more authentic and transferable.
success_criteria: States a purpose for their design (what it is for or what problem it solves)
Generates at least one idea for a solution to that purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a purpose-grounded design idea, Node 2 (communicating a design idea) and Node 3 (making) have no design intent to express or realise — purposeless communication and making is construction play, not design.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can communicate a design idea through drawing or modelling
nodes.minimum_width: Represent a design idea through at least one drawing or model
nodes.typical_width: Communicate a design idea using drawing or modelling; include basic features or labels; explain the design idea to others
wider: Draw or model a ramp design for rolling a ball or toy car — show key features and explain how the design serves the purpose
Model a design for a greenhouse or trellis using available materials — describe what each part is for

response_modes.reason: Design communication at Foundation requires students to externalise a mental idea into a physical representation. This is a challenging early skill — the gap between what students imagine and what they can draw or model is significant. Repeated practice across different design contexts builds fluency in using drawing/modelling as a thinking and communication tool.

success_criteria: Produces a drawing or model that represents their design idea
Can explain at least one feature of the drawing or model
nodes.hinge_reason: The communicated design idea is the raw material for Node 3 making — without an externalised representation, making is undirected and cannot be checked against a design intent. Node 3 requires something to make toward.

nodes.label: Making a solution safely
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use materials, equipment and steps to safely make a designed solution
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one material and one piece of equipment to make a solution; follow safety expectations for the tools or equipment used
nodes.typical_width: Use materials, components and equipment to make a solution across multiple construction contexts (joining, assembling, constructing); follow safety expectations; check that the solution functions as planned
wider: Use available or re-used materials in construction play — for example blocks, rain gutters or cardboard to make a ramp; explore how different materials affect how the solution works
Make and test a bowling, stacking or obstacle game with discarded food containers — assemble components and check they function as planned

response_modes.reason: Safe use of materials and equipment is a procedural and behavioural skill requiring consistent practice. Joining techniques, safe cutting, careful assembly — these need repetition across different making contexts before students can execute safely without active teacher supervision. Consolidation is the primary response; width adds variety of materials and contexts.

success_criteria: Uses at least one material and one tool or piece of equipment
Follows safety expectations for the tools and materials used

nodes.label: Evaluating the solution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate what they made using personal preferences
nodes.minimum_width: Share at least one opinion about their design or solution — what they like, what worked or what they would change
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the solution using personal preferences — describe what works well and what could be improved; use a simple evaluation tool (e.g. smiley face Likert scale) to record a judgement; connect evaluation to the original purpose
wider: Record evaluation using audio-recording or video-recording software — describe design strengths and weaknesses and what they would change
Explain how the equipment in a playground might be unsuitable for some children and suggest areas for design improvement — connecting personal evaluation to broader user needs

response_modes.reason: Evaluation at Foundation requires students to step back from making and judge their output against something — a preference, a purpose, a criterion. Without scaffolding, students tend to say 'I like it' without connecting to purpose or identifying anything to improve. A question structure (what did you want it to do? did it? what would you change?) builds evaluative reasoning rather than just approval.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The audio/video recording direction makes evaluation visible and revisitable — students can hear themselves reason, which is metacognitively richer than a smiley face scale alone. The playground accessibility direction extends evaluation from personal preference to user-centred reasoning.
success_criteria: Shares at least one opinion about their design or solution
Opinion is connected to the design — not just 'I like it' in general
